raw_text:
### Introduction and Pathophysiology
Cardiac amyloidosis (CA) is a progressive infiltrative cardiomyopathy characterized by extracellular deposition of misfolded protein fibrils within the myocardium [1]. Under polarized light microscopy, these fibrils display a characteristic apple-green birefringence when stained with Congo red [2]. While systemic amyloidosis can involve multiple organs [3], cardiac infiltration is the primary driver of patient morbidity and mortality [4]. The three main systemic amyloid types affecting the heart are immunoglobulin light-chain (AL) amyloidosis, wild-type transthyretin (ATTRwt) amyloidosis, and variant/hereditary transthyretin (ATTRv) amyloidosis [5]. 

AL amyloidosis, driven by a clonal plasma cell dyscrasia, represents a medical emergency due to rapidly progressive cardiac dysfunction [6]. In contrast, ATTRwt results from the age-related misfolding of wild-type transthyretin, typically presenting as a restrictive cardiomyopathy in elderly males [4]. ATTRv is caused by autosomal dominant mutations in the transthyretin (*TTR*) gene, manifesting with variable combinations of cardiomyopathy and polyneuropathy [3]. Extracardiac "red flags"—such as bilateral carpal tunnel syndrome, lumbar spinal stenosis, or spontaneous biceps tendon rupture—often precede cardiac symptoms by several years, particularly in ATTR [7].

### Clinical Staging and Risk Stratification
Prognostication is crucial in CA, given the vastly different treatment approaches for AL and ATTR. For AL amyloidosis, patient staging has historically relied on serum troponins and N-terminal pro-B-type natriuretic peptide (NT-proBNP) [8,9]. The revised Mayo Clinic staging system incorporates the difference between involved and uninvolved serum free light chains (dFLC) alongside these cardiac biomarkers to improve risk stratification [10]. For ATTR amyloidosis, the National Amyloidosis Centre (NAC) staging system classifies patients into three prognostic stages based on NT-proBNP and estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) [11], providing robust evaluation across both wild-type and variant cohorts [4].

### Diagnostic Imaging and Algorithm
Echocardiography remains the primary initial screening tool [4]. Classic findings include concentric ventricular wall thickening, biatrial enlargement, and restrictive diastolic filling [4]. Myocardial deformation analysis using two-dimensional speckle-tracking echocardiography characteristically demonstrates a relative "apical sparing" pattern, where longitudinal strain is preserved in the apex compared to the basal and mid-ventricular segments [12]. 

Cardiovascular magnetic resonance (CMR) imaging offers superior tissue characterization [4]. On CMR, diffuse subendocardial or transmural late gadolinium enhancement (LGE) is highly characteristic of CA [13]. Furthermore, native T1 mapping and calculated myocardial extracellular volume (ECV) fraction allow non-invasive quantification of amyloid burden, holding significant diagnostic and prognostic value in both AL and ATTR subtypes [14].

Technetium-labeled bone scintigraphy (using 99mTc-pyrophosphate, -DPD, or -hydroxymethylene diphosphonate) has revolutionized the diagnosis of ATTR-CA [15]. Based on the Perugini grading system, myocardial tracer uptake equal to or greater than rib uptake (Grade 2 or 3) is highly specific for ATTR [15]. This enabled the validation of a landmark non-biopsy diagnostic algorithm: in patients with clinical suspicion of CA, a Grade 2 or 3 bone scan in the absolute absence of a clonal plasma cell dyscrasia (confirmed via serum/urine immunofixation and serum free light chain assay) is sufficient to confirm ATTR-CA without requiring endomyocardial biopsy [16].

### Therapeutic Management
Managing CA involves a dual approach: supportive care and disease-modifying therapies [17]. Guideline-directed medical therapy for heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (e.g., beta-blockers and angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors) is poorly tolerated and often contraindicated in CA due to restrictive physiology and dependence on heart rate to maintain cardiac output [18]. Instead, loop diuretics and aldosterone antagonists are key to volume management [19]. 

For AL-CA, therapies aim to eliminate the underlying plasma cell clone [20] and achieve a deep hematologic and organ response [21]. The phase 3 ANDROMEDA trial established the combination of daratumumab (a CD38-targeted monoclonal antibody) with bortezomib, cyclophosphamide, and dexamethasone (Dara-CyBorD) as the first-line standard of care, yielding rapid and deep hematologic responses [22]. Selected eligible patients may also undergo autologous stem cell transplantation [20].

For ATTR-CA, therapeutic strategies target the production, stability, or clearance of TTR [4]. Tafamidis, an oral small-molecule kinetic stabilizer that binds to the thyroxine-binding sites of the TTR tetramer, was the first drug shown to reduce all-cause mortality and cardiovascular hospitalizations in the ATTR-ACT trial [23]. More recently, the phase 3 ATTRibute-CM trial demonstrated that acoramidis, a high-affinity TTR stabilizer achieving >90% ex vivo stabilization, significantly improved hierarchical composite endpoints [24]. 

Gene silencing therapies represent another major breakthrough. In the HELIOS-B trial, vutrisiran, a subcutaneously administered small interfering RNA (siRNA) targeting hepatic TTR production, reduced the risk of all-cause mortality and recurrent cardiovascular events [25]. Similarly, patisiran (an intravenous siRNA) and inotersen (a subcutaneously administered antisense oligonucleotide) have demonstrated efficacy in slowing polyneuropathy progression and stabilizing cardiac parameters in ATTRv [26,27,28]. Eplontersen, a ligand-conjugated antisense oligonucleotide, also showed significant TTR suppression and clinical benefits in ATTRv polyneuropathy [29]. Finally, in vivo gene editing using CRISPR-Cas9 (NTLA-2001) has entered clinical development, offering the potential for a single-dose, permanent knockout of hepatic TTR production [30].

### Conclusion
The landscape of cardiac amyloidosis has undergone a profound paradigm shift over the past decade. Early recognition through multimodality imaging, non-invasive diagnostic algorithms, and the advent of highly effective, targeted therapies are transforming CA from a historically terminal disease to a manageable chronic condition. Ongoing clinical trials will further define the roles of combination or sequential therapies in optimizing long-term survival.
